doc.title: Jimmy Wormworth interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 6, 2002

title: Later listening: Mulligan, Brubeck and discovering Charlie Parker
summary: He moves on to Mulligan, Shorty Rogers and Brubeck, then Charlie Parker and hard bop.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And it just sort of went on from there. I really can’t remember what influenced me after the period where I first discovered those Nat Cole and Art Tatum and Nellie Lutcher records. There was a period like I guess from the time I was 12 or so to when I started playing that I don’t remember listening to any newer records. Around 14 I started getting interested in some of Gerry Mulligan’s work and Shorty Rogers’ Giants, And that’s when I started trying to write, when I was about 15 or 16. But that interested me. And Dave Brubeck’s octet interested me for a while. And then I think by the time I was 16 or so, that was when I met Gordon Smith and Ernie Washington and Sal Amico and those guys and they told me well look man, you’ve heard of Charlie Parker, now you’re going to have to check him out. And the first time I heart Charlie Parker and Dizzy or whoever, it sounded so futuristic to me. I could tell that technically it was virtuosity, but I don’t think artistically it made an immediate impression on me. But it wasn’t long after that that it did. And to me Charlie Parker and Louis Armstrong and Duke Ellington are — what do you call them — the beacons of the music? The arbiter? It took me to middle age before I could appreciate artists from the period of music that came before the period I grew into, except for Art Tatum and — well Art Tatum to me was the precursor of Bebop. And Nat Cole already could be considered a Bebop player. To me he grew out of that Earl Hines school. To me there were two schools, the Art Tatum percussive school and the Earl Hines lyrical sort of flowery school. And to me Bud Powell came from the Art Tatum school and Tommy Flanagan or Nat Cole came from the Earl Hines school. But well Charlie Parker, without much time put in listening to him, just mesmerized me. I mean he was definitely a musical genius. And then I was just really hooked on the music that started with him and came after, the so-called hard bop.
